description: We’re a two-person interdisciplinary team: a computer engineering student and an archaeology student exploring space archaeology, treating hardware left on the Moon and Mars as heritage sites. For “Abandoned but not Forgotten,” we’re building an interactive atlas that catalogs these objects like museum artifacts, shows them through NASA orbital imagery and tells their stories. We combine coding with archaeological expertise. Our team is complete.
summary: MERISO is an interactive "space archaeology atlas" that turns the hardware NASA left on the Moon and Mars into a museum collection for school-age children. Kids choose a research region (Moon or Mars), spin a realistic 3D globe and explore 13 dig sites placed at their real landing coordinates – from the Apollo 11 descent stage and Surveyor 3 to Sojourner, Spirit, InSight and the Ingenuity helicopter. Each site opens an artifact card that answers four archaeological questions: What is it? What did it teach us? What condition is it in today? What don't we know yet? A "time machine" uses taphonomy – the science of how objects decay – to show how each artifact will change after 1,000, 10,000 and 1 million years under each world's real conditions: UV radiation and micrometeorites on the Moon, wind, dust and burial on Mars. Measured facts and scientific projections are clearly labelled, and every card links to its sources. The project tells the story of "abandoned but not forgotten" equipment and teaches children to see it as humanity's first off-world heritage. It is bilingual (English/Turkish), gamified with quizzes, badges and a field journal, and runs in any browser on desktop or phone
details:
THE CHALLENGE AND OUR SOLUTION

The "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge asks how to tell the story of the equipment NASA left on the Moon and Mars. Most children don't know these landers, rovers and flags are still out there, and the information that exists is scattered across technical mission pages written for experts. Our solution is to treat every piece of hardware as an archaeological artifact and every landing site as a dig site, then present them in an interactive, museum-style atlas that children can explore on their own.

WHAT IT DOES

MERISO is a web-based space archaeology simulation. Users pick the Moon or Mars, rotate a 3D globe with the mouse or finger, and find 13 dig sites at their real coordinates. Hovering over a site shows a small "find tag"; clicking it opens an artifact card with a 3D model, a dig-site plan, the artifact's story, its current condition, open questions and source links.

The core feature is the Time Machine. Based on taphonomy (the study of how remains decay over time), the 3D artifact visibly changes at +1,000, +10,000 and +1,000,000 years: on the Moon, UV bleaching, micrometeorite pitting and very slow dust cover; on Mars, red dust coating, wind abrasion and sand burial. Projections are labelled as projections, so children learn to separate measured evidence from scientific estimates.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Makes children aware that this equipment still exists and is part of humanity's heritage.

- Teaches the archaeologist's way of thinking: observe, record, ask what is still unknown.

- Texts are written so an 8-year-old can follow them while adults stay engaged.

- Gamification (quizzes, badges, field journal and a robot guide called Digby) turns learning into exploration.

- Bilingual (EN/TR), free, no sign-up, works on desktop and mobile.

HOW WE BUILT IT

- HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules), no backend.

- Three.js (WebGL) for the globes and 3D models; GLTFLoader with Meshopt for NASA 3D models.

- Custom GLSL shader effects for decay (dust, bleaching, pitting, frost) and terrain displacement for burial.

- Real landing coordinates converted to positions on the 3D sphere.

- Hosted as a static site on Vercel.

CREATIVITY AND TEAM

Our team brings together computer engineering and archaeology. Instead of treating abandoned hardware as space junk, we treated it like an archaeologist treats a site: artifact cards, stratigraphy-style time layers, dig plans and honest "we don't know yet" notes. We focused on scientific accuracy (every fact is sourced), age-appropriate language and a playful, museum-like design.

WHY OUR APPROACH STANDS OUT

- It tells the story of the past and the future: other approaches show what the hardware looked like when it landed; the Time Machine also shows what will happen to it, using the science of taphonomy and the real environment of each world.

- Real archaeology, not just space facts: an archaeology student on the team shaped the content, so children learn a real scientific method (observe, record, question) instead of memorising facts.

- Honest science for kids: every card separates what is measured from what is projected and links to its NASA sources, which builds trust and critical thinking.

- Easy to reach: it runs in any browser on desktop or phone, with no installation, no account and no cost, in two languages, so any classroom can use it right away.
